stages.ask: Why did the Industrial Revolution start in Britain?

explain.say: In September 1830 the world's first intercity railway with timetabled steam trains opened between Liverpool and Manchester. Raw cotton from the port could now reach the mills in about two hours. Look at the chain. Coal fed steam engines, steam engines drove factories, and factories needed railways. How did one small island start all this?

explain.say: See the reasons. Britain had coal near the surface, so energy was cheap. The economic historian Robert Allen adds that British wages were high, so a machine that saved workers paid for itself. Joel Mokyr stresses a culture of tinkerers sharing useful knowledge. Which do you find most convincing, the coal or the culture?

explain.say: Now real numbers. This graph shows each region's share of world manufacturing, from Paul Bairoch's estimates. In 1750 China and India made more than half the world's goods; Britain under 2 percent. By 1880 Britain made about 23 percent and India under 3. Kenneth Pomeranz calls this split the Great Divergence. Which line falls fastest after 1830?

Look at the map. Machines spread from Lancashire to Belgium, the German Ruhr and New England, and after 1868 to Japan. Pomeranz argues Britain's luck in coal and colonies mattered most, while India's handloom weavers lost markets to cheap machine cloth under colonial rule. Why would a colony struggle to protect its own industries?

The human side was hard. Manchester grew from about 75,000 people in 1801 to about 300,000 by 1851, with child labour and crowded, unhealthy streets that Friedrich Engels described in 1845. Optimists stress rising long-run wages; pessimists stress those hungry decades. Great work. Exam tip: say which workers, which years, and which measure.

faq.q: Why did the Industrial Revolution start in Britain?
faq.a: Historians point to cheap coal near the surface, high wages that made labour-saving machines profitable (Robert Allen), a culture of practical science and invention (Joel Mokyr), large markets including the empire and Atlantic trade, and stable institutions such as banks and patents.

The term, made famous by Kenneth Pomeranz in 2000, for the way Western Europe's economy pulled ahead of China, India and the rest of the world in the nineteenth century, after centuries of rough similarity in the richest regions.

faq.q: Did the Industrial Revolution make workers better off?
faq.a: This is the standard of living debate. Optimists point to rising real wages after about 1830 to 1850; pessimists point to long hours, child labour, crowded cities and shorter lives in industrial towns in the early decades. The answer depends on period, region and measure.
asks: What is the standard of living debate?

faq.a: Watt did not invent the steam engine, but in 1769 he patented a separate condenser that made Newcomen's engine far more efficient, and later added rotary motion so engines could drive mill machinery.

India was a leading maker of cotton cloth in 1750. Cheap British machine-made textiles, colonial trade policies and tariffs favouring Britain helped shrink India's share of world manufacturing to under 3 percent by 1880, by Bairoch's estimates.

facts: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in September 1830.
Paul Bairoch estimated Britain's share of world manufacturing at about 23 percent in 1880.
Engels published The Condition of the Working Class in England in 1845.

quiz.say: By Bairoch's estimates, Britain's share of world manufacturing rose from 1.9 percent in 1750 to 22.9 percent in 1880. About how many times bigger is that?
quiz.show: 1.9% to 22.9% is about how many times bigger?

wrong.2: Fifty times 1.9 would be 95 percent, almost all world industry.
